risks.risk: Imported raw material price and currency volatility
risks.note: SSP fertilisers are based on imported raw materials (rock phosphate, sulphur) which can face severe volatility in prices and foreign currency exchange rates, directly affecting the Company's profitability.

risks.risk: Sulphur cost spike has idled capacity
risks.note: A continuous, sharp rise in Sulphur prices following the west Asia crisis made Sulphur-based SSP production unviable, forcing the Company to shut fertilizer operations at its Jhansi and Malwan units; these remain shut and adversely impacted by prevailing freight subsidy policy, with resumption contingent on the situation normalizing.

The business is greatly affected by monsoons; performance depends on rainfall timing and adequacy, and the monsoon for 2026 is forecast to be normal only in the first half (June-July) and below normal thereafter (August-September), which can adversely impact the fertilizer division.

SSP is a subsidised product and the Company's realisations and profitability are tied to Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates set by the Government and the pace of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) reform; delays in government subsidy disbursement are explicitly flagged as a concern.

The NBS policy has attracted new entrants to the SSP market; combined with overall weak market conditions, this has created excess supply, changing consumption and stocking patterns that necessitate higher inventories for the Company.

risks.risk: Seasonal demand concentration and working-capital intensity
risks.note: Fertilizer consumption is concentrated mainly in two months each of the Kharif and Rabi seasons, and this seasonality, combined with volatile raw material markets and logistics costs, drives a higher requirement of working capital.

risks.risk: Low farmer awareness / logistics constraints limiting SSP adoption
risks.note: Lack of awareness of the benefits of SSP consumption amongst farmers, together with logistics availability and cost, is flagged as a continuing concern for the SSP industry and the Company despite SSP being the lowest-cost fertilizer option.

one-line thesis: Khaitan Chemicals faces severe margin pressure on its core SSP business due to soaring sulphur prices and capped retail pricing, despite improved EBITDA from sulphuric acid and subsidy hikes; liquidity remains fragile with thin cash balances and high working capital dependency, making its financial stability contingent on timely subsidy disbursement and ability to pass on costs.
financial scorecard / credit view: Revenue: INR 8,237M (FY25); EBITDA: INR 1,216M (FY25); PAT: Not disclosed; Net Debt: INR 1,828M (FY25); Credit Rating: Ind-Ra, IND BBB-, Rating Watch with Developing Implications; Rationale: Constrained financial flexibility, thin SSP profitability amid raw material inflation, high working capital utilization (84%), and subsidy-dependent cash flows.
guidance / outlook: Outlook hinges on ability to raise SSP retail prices without losing volume, consistent raw material supply, and timely subsidy releases; no formal guidance issued beyond monitoring these factors.
order book & pipeline: Not disclosed; sales volume for SSP was 0.38 mt in 9MFY26, up from 0.34 mt in FY24, but production halted at three plants due to cost constraints.
segment / subsidiary detail: SSP: 88% of revenue (FY25), 1.13 mtpa capacity, 44% utilization in 9MFY26; Sulphuric Acid: 11% of revenue, EBITDA/ton rose to INR 3,852 in 9MFY26 from INR 2,068 in FY25; by-product steam powers 4.32MW unit.
growth verticals / optionality: None identified; expansion constrained by capital intensity, subsidy dependency, and raw material volatility; potential upside only if SSP pricing power is restored and sulphur costs stabilize.
margins & cost dynamics: SSP gross margin: negative under current subsidy (INR 8,149/ton) vs. cost of INR 15,500–16,500/ton (raw material + manufacturing); SA margin improved significantly due to higher realized prices and lower input costs relative to SSP.
capex / expansion: Not disclosed; no new capacity announced; focus appears to be on maintaining existing operations amid financial stress.
capital allocation: Prioritizing working capital needs and debt servicing; no dividends or buybacks indicated; reliance on related-party loans (INR 220M as of 9MFY26) to manage liquidity.
risks & watch-items: 1. Sulphur price volatility (USD 500–600/ton vs. FY25 avg USD 150–160); 2. Delayed or reduced government subsidy disbursement; 3. Capped DAP prices limiting SSP price flexibility; 4. High working capital utilization (84%) and low cash balance (INR 0.8M); 5. Geopolitical disruption in West Asia affecting raw material supply.
non-obvious takeaways: Despite negative EBITDA in prior years, KCFL's profitability in 9MFY26 was driven by a one-time subsidy jump (NBS increased from INR 5,122 to INR 8,149/ton), masking structural cost issues; sulphuric acid margins are a hidden bright spot but too small to offset SSP losses.

themes.title: Fertilizer subsidy & nutrient-policy cycle
themes.need: Fertilizer makers are driven by NBS/urea subsidy policy, gas-pooling and nutrient pricing rather than the crop-protection volume/molecule-launch recovery. Q1FY27's supply-side read comes from MBAPL: revenue roughly flat at INR 416cr with EBITDA +16% and PAT +17% purely on cheap March-bought raw material that management said is now EXHAUSTED, with utilisation only ~43-45% because of raw-material availability rather than demand - SSP sales were +28% and NPK +33% YoY against production down 7%/28%. Its Dhule (Maharashtra) integrated complex commissions +3,30,000 MTPA DAP-NPK plus 99,000 MTPA phosphoric acid in Oct-2026 and a second phase in Oct-2027, framed as a >50% turnover jump toward ~INR 3,500cr revenue and 15.6 lakh MT capacity by FY28; Egypt/Jordan rock-phosphate sourcing (non-Hormuz) insulated it relative to import-dependent peers. Subsidy clarity and gas costs still set the near-term margin.
themes.driver: NBS/urea subsidy policy (the Oct-Mar rate revision), gas-pooling and nutrient pricing; MBAPL's Oct-2026 Dhule commissioning and the utilisation ramp toward ~90%; kharif demand pull-through after a delayed monsoon.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Fertilizer demand is closely tied to monsoon performance and government subsidy (NBS/DBT) policy
- SSP is expected to see sustained demand given its suitability across various soil and crop types, and government intent to encourage SSP as a substitute for imported DAP and NPK
- Continued rise in Sulphur prices (following the west Asia crisis) is pressuring input costs, partially offset by enhanced Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) support from the Government for Kharif 2025 and Rabi 2025
- Management expects performance to improve in the long term as the west Asia crisis resolves, leveraging the Company's high integrated capacity, multi-geographical locations and established brands
- Monsoon for 2026 is forecast to be normal in June-July but below normal in August-September, which could adversely impact the fertilizer division
- NBS policy has attracted new entrants into the market, creating excess supply and changing consumption/stocking patterns that necessitate higher inventories
- SSP raw materials are largely imported, exposing the Company to raw material price and foreign currency volatility

margins.body: SSP gross margin: negative under current subsidy (INR 8,149/ton) vs. cost of INR 15,500–16,500/ton (raw material + manufacturing); SA margin improved significantly due to higher realized prices and lower input costs relative to SSP.

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Subsidy policy] The slide headed "Kharif 2026 Fertilizer Subsidy Update" states INR 41,533.81 Cr of P&K subsidy approved by the Union Cabinet for Rabi 2025-26, INR 3,582 Cr higher than Rabi 2025; per-kg nutrient subsidy (Kharif 2026) of N 47.32 (+10% vs Rabi 2025), P 52.76 (+10%), K 2.38 and S 3.16 (+10%). SSP freight subsidy continued; DAP retail price kept stable at Rs 1,350 per 50 kg bag.
- [Demand driver] DAP import disruption is the stated tailwind: India imports over 50% of key fertilizer raw materials, 2025 DAP imports were hit by China's export curbs, and India signed a 5-year deal with Saudi Arabia to import 3.1 million tonnes of DAP; government and associations are "educating farmers to look at SSP as an alternative".
- [Discontinued operations] FY26 shows a loss from discontinued operations of INR (42) Mn and INR 43 Mn of assets/disposal group classified as held for sale; the 2012 milestone records exit from the soya business (Ratlam and TriStar units) "due to declining profitability in the soya oil segment across India", with a significant portion of the land retained.
- [Ownership] Shareholding as on 31st March 2026: Promoters 72.65%, Public 27.01%, FII 0.34%; market cap INR 4,191.87 Mn, 96.99 Mn shares outstanding, CMP INR 43.22 against a 52-week high/low of 136.00/42.80.
- [Market context] SSP accounts for 10.00% of India's fertilizer consumption (Urea 55.00%, DAP 15.00%, NPK 15.00%, Speciality 5.00%); the Indian fertilizer market is projected to reach USD 16.6 billion by 2032, and India is the second-largest fertilizer consumer at 60 million MT/year with 50% raw material imports.
